_README: Structure and metadata for the annotated English edition of 一触即发 (On a Hair Trigger) by Zhang Yong. Flat structure: a prologue (楔子) + 35 chapters; the source's own cover page and 目录 are dropped because the builder regenerates a title page and a full hyperlinked contents. Chapter-title renderings are provisional literary versions of the 7-character couplet headings, to be finalized (with their classical allusions footnoted) during translation.
description: A period espionage novel set in the Shanghai of the 1910s to 1930s. Twin brothers, separated in infancy, are swept into the shadow war among rival intelligence services and a Japanese conspiracy known as the “Thunder Plan.” The opening work of Zhang Yong’s acclaimed “spy trilogy” (with The Disguiser and Seamless), later adapted for television.
_source_note: Source: a digital EPUB (Calibre-repackaged EasyPub text; internal timestamp 2015) of 一触即发. Reliable Unicode text, no OCR. One embedded image (the cover). Chapters are continuous prose with a single h2 couplet heading each; scene breaks are blank paragraphs, not sub-sections, so the logical structure is flat. The novel was first written in 2009; the book edition used for metadata is the Lijiang Publishing House edition (2012-10).
_translator_note: Rendered verbatim as the Translator's Note back-matter page.
translator_note: This is an English translation of 一触即发 (On a Hair Trigger) by Zhang Yong (张勇), the first novel of her “spy trilogy,” a period espionage story set in early twentieth-century Shanghai.

The chapter titles are seven-character couplet lines in the classical manner, several of them quotations from or allusions to Tang and Song poems and others the author's own pastiche; they are given here in literary renderings, and their sources, where traceable, are set out in the notes.

The source text is translated in full; a paragraph-by-paragraph bilingual audit file is kept alongside this edition. Names follow pinyin except where a conventional English form exists; renderings marked provisional in the glossary are romanizations not attested in English-language scholarship. Notes are the translator's throughout, and where a passage is genuinely ambiguous the choice is stated in a note rather than smoothed over.
